html:
The Taíno were the Indigenous peoples of most of the Caribbean islands when Europeans arrived: the Bahamas, Cuba, Jamaica, Hispaniola, Puerto Rico and the northern Lesser Antilles. They spoke an Arawakan language and are also called Island Arawaks.

They were farmers. They grew cassava, sweet potatoes, maize and cotton in mounded fields, fished from large dugout canoes, and lived in fixed villages ruled by chiefs called caciques. Rank and inheritance passed through the mother's line. Their religion centred on zemis, spirits and the carved objects that held them. Taíno words reached English through Spanish: canoe, hammock, hurricane, barbecue and maize.

They shared the islands with older peoples such as the Guanahatabey of western Cuba and the Ciguayo of Hispaniola, and fought the Kalinago newcomers of the islands to the southeast.

In 1492 Christopher Columbus landed among the Lucayan Taíno of the Bahamas (see Columbus reaches the Caribbean). Spanish rule on Hispaniola brought forced labour, war, hunger and new diseases, and the Taíno population collapsed within a few decades. Bartolomé de las Casas wrote of their suffering. Taíno ancestry and words live on in Cuba, Puerto Rico and the Dominican Republic, and in Taíno revival communities today.
